## Purpose

This document explores the threatened fauna data and identifies which species have enough usable spatial records for further analysis.

## Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

fauna <- read_csv("../data/meeting1/vba_threatened_fauna_melbourne_fringe.csv")

glimpse(fauna)
```
```{r}
fauna_species_summary <- fauna |>
  group_by(comm_name, sci_name) |>
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    earliest_record = min(start_year, na.rm = TRUE),
    latest_record = max(start_year, na.rm = TRUE),
    ffg_status = paste(unique(na.omit(ffg_desc)), collapse = "; "),
    epbc_status = paste(unique(na.omit(epbc_desc)), collapse = "; "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_records))

fauna_species_summary
```


```{r}
fauna |>
  summarise(
    total_records = n(),
    missing_longitude = sum(is.na(longitude)),
    missing_latitude = sum(is.na(latitude)),
    usable_coordinates = sum(!is.na(longitude) & !is.na(latitude))
  )
```

## Spatial distribution across study LGAs

```{r}
# Load LGA boundaries
lga_boundary <- st_read(
  "../data/LGA_2025_AUST_GDA2020/LGA_2025_AUST_GDA2020.shp",
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Keep only the five study LGAs
study_lga <- lga_boundary |>
  filter(LGA_NAME25 %in% c(
    "Casey",
    "Hume",
    "Melton",
    "Whittlesea",
    "Wyndham"
  ))

# Convert fauna records to spatial points
fauna_sf <- fauna |>
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
    crs = 4326,
    remove = FALSE
  )

# Match coordinate system with the LGA boundaries
fauna_sf <- st_transform(fauna_sf, st_crs(study_lga))

# Assign fauna records to LGAs
fauna_lga <- st_join(
  fauna_sf,
  study_lga |> select(LGA_NAME25),
  join = st_within
)

# Check how many records fall within each study LGA
fauna_lga |>
  count(LGA_NAME25, sort = TRUE)
```



```{r}
fauna_lga |>
  summarise(
    total_records = n(),
    inside_study_lgas = sum(!is.na(LGA_NAME25)),
    outside_study_lgas = sum(is.na(LGA_NAME25))
  )
```

```{r}
species_by_lga <- fauna_lga |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(LGA_NAME25)) |>
  count(comm_name, sci_name, LGA_NAME25, sort = TRUE)

species_by_lga
```

```{r}
species_lga_summary <- fauna_lga |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(LGA_NAME25)) |>
  group_by(comm_name, sci_name) |>
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_lgas = n_distinct(LGA_NAME25),
    lgas = paste(sort(unique(LGA_NAME25)), collapse = ", "),
    earliest_record = min(start_year, na.rm = TRUE),
    latest_record = max(start_year, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_records))

species_lga_summary
```

### Initial finding

The supplied threatened-fauna extract appears insufficient for detailed species-level spatial analysis. Most species are represented by relatively few records and are concentrated within a single study LGA.

Golden Sun Moth currently has the strongest spatial coverage, with 18 records across Hume, Whittlesea and Wyndham. Southern Brown Bandicoot has only five records, all within Casey.

Additional VBA and/or Atlas of Living Australia occurrence records should therefore be investigated before finalising the focal species for detailed analysis.


## Candidate species screening using ALA data

Because the supplied VBA fauna extract contained relatively few records within the study LGAs, four candidate threatened species were further examined using Atlas of Living Australia occurrence data. The ALA datasets were spatially filtered to Casey, Hume, Melton, Whittlesea and Wyndham in `R/02_species_data.R`.

Recent records from 2015 onwards were then compared to assess whether each species had sufficient contemporary spatial coverage for further analysis.

Based on the ALA candidate datasets, Golden Sun Moth and Growling Grass Frog currently provide the strongest basis for further spatial analysis. Since 2015, Golden Sun Moth has 4,550 records across four study LGAs, while Growling Grass Frog has 1,891 records across all five. Southern Brown Bandicoot is highly concentrated within Casey, while Striped Legless Lizard records are concentrated mainly within Melton and occur across only three study LGAs.

Golden Sun Moth and Growling Grass Frog are therefore retained as the leading focal-species candidates, pending comparison with the broader high-accuracy VBA dataset.

## Habitat Value analysis

```{r}
library(terra)

habitat <- rast(
  "../data/habitat_value/habitat_value_75m_20241024_vg2020.tif"
)

habitat
```

```{r}
study_lga_vect <- vect(study_lga)

study_lga_vect <- project(
  study_lga_vect,
  crs(habitat)
)

habitat_study <- crop(
  habitat,
  study_lga_vect
)

habitat_study <- mask(
  habitat_study,
  study_lga_vect
)

habitat_study
```

```{r}
plot(habitat_study)
plot(study_lga_vect, add = TRUE)
```

```{r}
habitat_by_lga <- terra::extract(
  habitat,
  study_lga_vect,
  fun = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

habitat_by_lga
```

```{r}
habitat_by_lga$LGA_NAME25 <- study_lga_vect$LGA_NAME25

habitat_by_lga <- habitat_by_lga |>
  select(LGA_NAME25, everything())

habitat_by_lga
```

```{r}
high_habitat_study <- habitat_study >= 70

high_habitat_by_lga <- terra::extract(
  high_habitat,
  study_lga_vect,
  fun = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

high_habitat_by_lga$LGA_NAME25 <- study_lga_vect$LGA_NAME25

high_habitat_by_lga <- high_habitat_by_lga |>
  select(LGA_NAME25, everything()) |>
  mutate(
    high_habitat_percent = habitat_value_75m_20241024_vg2020 * 100
  )

high_habitat_by_lga
```
A provisional threshold of Habitat Value ≥ 70 was used to identify relatively high-value habitat for exploratory comparison. 
Using a threshold of Habitat Value ≥ 70, Wyndham has the largest proportion of high-value habitat (43.55%), followed by Melton (41.79%), Whittlesea (33.62%), Hume (29.94%) and Casey (15.93%). This suggests that Wyndham and Melton may contain particularly important biodiversity areas within the study region and should be examined closely when compared with urban expansion pressure and threatened-fauna occurrence.


## High-accuracy VBA fauna validation

```{r}
vba_full <- st_read(
  "../data/FLORAFAUNA1/VBA_FAUNA25.shp",
  quiet = TRUE
)

vba_full
```
```{r}
vba_study <- st_join(
  vba_full,
  study_lga |> select(LGA_NAME25),
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)

vba_study
```

```{r}
vba_candidates <- vba_study |>
  filter(
    COMM_NAME %in% c(
      "Golden Sun Moth",
      "Growling Grass Frog",
      "Southern Brown Bandicoot",
      "Striped Legless Lizard"
    )
  )

vba_candidates |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(COMM_NAME, sort = TRUE)
```
```{r}
vba_candidate_summary <- vba_candidates |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(COMM_NAME) |>
  summarise(
    total_records = n(),
    n_lgas = n_distinct(LGA_NAME25),
    lgas = paste(sort(unique(LGA_NAME25)), collapse = ", "),
    earliest_year = min(START_YEAR, na.rm = TRUE),
    latest_year = max(START_YEAR, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_records))

vba_candidate_summary
```

```{r}
vba_recent_summary <- vba_candidates |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(START_YEAR >= 2015) |>
  group_by(COMM_NAME) |>
  summarise(
    recent_records = n(),
    recent_lgas = n_distinct(LGA_NAME25),
    lgas = paste(sort(unique(LGA_NAME25)), collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(recent_records))

vba_recent_summary
```
The high-accuracy VBA dataset supports the selection of Golden Sun Moth and Growling Grass Frog as the two focal species. Golden Sun Moth has the strongest recent representation, with 2,899 records since 2015 across four study LGAs. Growling Grass Frog has fewer recent records but maintains broader spatial relevance across multiple growth corridors. In contrast, Southern Brown Bandicoot records are concentrated entirely within Casey, while Striped Legless Lizard has more limited spatial coverage. Golden Sun Moth and Growling Grass Frog were therefore selected for the subsequent biodiversity and habitat analyses.


## BCS Conservation Areas analysis

```{r}
bcs <- st_read(
  "../data/BCS_Conservation_Areas/ll_gda2020/esrishape/whole_of_dataset/victoria/FLORAFAUNA1/MSA_BCS_CONS_AREA.shp",
  quiet = TRUE
)

bcs
```
```{r}
bcs_study <- st_intersection(
  bcs,
  study_lga |> select(LGA_NAME25)
)

bcs_study
```

```{r}
bcs_area_by_lga <- bcs_study |>
  mutate(
    area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6
  ) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(LGA_NAME25) |>
  summarise(
    bcs_area_km2 = sum(area_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_bcs_features = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bcs_area_by_lga
```

```{r}
lga_area <- study_lga |>
  mutate(
    lga_area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6
  ) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(LGA_NAME25, lga_area_km2)

bcs_summary <- bcs_area_by_lga |>
  left_join(lga_area, by = "LGA_NAME25") |>
  mutate(
    bcs_percent = (bcs_area_km2 / lga_area_km2) * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(bcs_percent))

bcs_summary
```

BCS Conservation Area coverage varies substantially across the five study LGAs. Whittlesea has the highest proportion of land within BCS Conservation Areas (3.52%), followed by Hume (2.99%) and Melton (2.08%). Wyndham has relatively limited BCS coverage (1.06%), while Casey has the lowest coverage (0.22%). When considered alongside the Habitat Value results, Wyndham may warrant closer examination because it contains a comparatively high proportion of high-value habitat but relatively low BCS conservation coverage.




```{r}
# Convert BCS to the same CRS as the Habitat Value raster
bcs_vect <- vect(bcs_study)
bcs_vect <- project(bcs_vect, crs(habitat))

# Create a raster mask for BCS conservation areas
bcs_mask <- rasterize(
  bcs_vect,
  habitat_study,
  field = 1,
  background = 0
)

# High-value habitat inside BCS
high_inside_bcs <- high_habitat_study * bcs_mask

# High-value habitat outside BCS
high_outside_bcs <- high_habitat_study * (1 - bcs_mask)
```

```{r}
inside_count <- global(high_inside_bcs, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]
outside_count <- global(high_outside_bcs, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]

total_high <- inside_count + outside_count

protection_gap_summary <- tibble(
  category = c("Inside BCS", "Outside BCS"),
  cells = c(inside_count, outside_count),
  percent = c(
    inside_count / total_high * 100,
    outside_count / total_high * 100
  )
)

protection_gap_summary
```
Only 3.81% of high-value habitat cells within the study area fall inside BCS Conservation Areas, while 96.19% lie outside them. This suggests a substantial potential protection gap, with most relatively high-value habitat not currently overlapping the existing BCS conservation network. These areas should be examined further alongside threatened-fauna occurrence and urban expansion pressure before identifying final priority areas for protection.

```{r}
focal_species <- vba_candidates |>
  filter(
    COMM_NAME %in% c(
      "Golden Sun Moth",
      "Growling Grass Frog"
    ),
    START_YEAR >= 2015
  )

species_bcs_overlap <- st_join(
  focal_species,
  bcs_study |> select(CA_NAME),
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
) |>
  mutate(
    bcs_status = if_else(
      is.na(CA_NAME),
      "Outside BCS",
      "Inside BCS"
    )
  )

species_bcs_summary <- species_bcs_overlap |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(COMM_NAME, bcs_status) |>
  group_by(COMM_NAME) |>
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100
  ) |>
  ungroup()

species_bcs_summary
```
Recent VBA records indicate that 39.43% of Golden Sun Moth observations occur within BCS Conservation Areas, while 60.57% occur outside them. In contrast, only 1.74% of recent Growling Grass Frog records fall within BCS areas, with 98.26% occurring outside. This suggests that Growling Grass Frog occurrences are particularly concentrated beyond the existing BCS conservation network, while Golden Sun Moth has greater but still incomplete overlap with designated conservation areas.


```{r}
# Transform focal species points to the Habitat Value raster CRS
focal_species_habitat <- st_transform(
  focal_species,
  crs(habitat)
)

# Extract Habitat Value at each species occurrence point
habitat_at_species <- terra::extract(
  habitat,
  vect(focal_species_habitat)
)

# Add extracted Habitat Value back to the species records
focal_species_habitat$habitat_value <- habitat_at_species[[2]]
```

```{r}
species_habitat_summary <- focal_species_habitat |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(COMM_NAME) |>
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    mean_habitat_value = mean(habitat_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_habitat_value = median(habitat_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    high_value_records = sum(habitat_value >= 70, na.rm = TRUE),
    high_value_percent = mean(habitat_value >= 70, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

species_habitat_summary
```

Recent focal-species records are strongly associated with higher Habitat Value, particularly for Growling Grass Frog. The mean Habitat Value at Growling Grass Frog occurrence locations is 87.34, with 86.34% of recent records occurring in areas with Habitat Value ≥70. Golden Sun Moth records also show substantial overlap with higher-value habitat, with a mean Habitat Value of 70.74 and 59.61% of recent records occurring in areas above the same threshold. These results suggest that both focal species are concentrated in ecologically valuable areas, with the pattern especially pronounced for Growling Grass Frog.
